Dear all,

I am relatively new to unmarked and occupancy modelling, and I have been searching this group for quite long time to try to answer come of my doubts.
Currently I am facing a doubt that I cannot solve, and perhaps more experienced people might be able to tell if I am doing something wrong.
I am trying to model amphibian roadkill through a dynamic occupancy model (using colext function) through a period of ~14 years in the same sampled roads (divided into 70 segments). Because amphibians are very season dependent, I am dividing the sampling in 2 seasons (of 6 months per year each - wet season (through 11 years) and dry season (14 years)), and in total I have 6 replicates per season within each year (one visit per month), over the primary sampling.
I have several siteCovs (e.g. land use covers) and yearlySiteCovs. And because my sampling periodicity changed over the years (daily or weekly) I have sampling effort and also precipitation as ObsCovs. I am currently interested in determine which covariates are responsible for amphibian roadkill (with the component of colonization and extintion as well) for each road segment.

I expected the models to perform worst in the dry season since I naturally have less observations (amphibians are more active during autumn), but I am having the opposite response (poor fit in wet season).

parts:
Hi Tiago,

You should be adding many more iterations to the goodness-of-fit test, e.g., 1000 or better yet, 10 000. Your P-value of 0 indicates that none of the bootstrapped samples had a chi-square value >= to the chi-square statistic from your data. Also note that if you run the analysis on a number of species, it is very likely that the model will not fit for some species with sparse data.

Best,

Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Strange p-values of zero in dynamic occupancy models
parts:
Dear Tiago,

fewer observations don't necessarily mean that you are less likely to get a fitting model in a GoF test like this --- in fact quite the contrary may be true: with less data you have less power to detect patterns that don't look right under your model and are thus less likely to obtain a significant GoF test.

The test output yields at least a little bit of insight into WHERE your model does not fit (at least with respect to time, but not with respect to sites). That is, where the differences between your observed data, and what the model says the data should look like, are greatest.

For the wet season, the total chi-square for the actual data is about 2100, while for a fitting model one would expect a value of about 580 (that's the median of the bootstrap distribution). The value for the full data set is obtained by summing the values of the test statistic over all the years. Thus, under a fitting model one would expect annual values of about 580 / 11 = 53. For the observed data, the chi-square contributions from years 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 look about OK, but for the other years there is strong lack of fit, mostly so in years 4, 7, 8 and 11. Perhaps you can now imagine some process that might have lead to something "special" in these seasons ? And perhaps you can then add a covariate that expresses that effect and in this way improve the fit of your model ?

Finally, you could also adopt what some might say is a dirty little trick, but what is widely done in the analysis of count data: claim that the lack of fit detected is just "overdispersion", or unstructured noise, rather than the result of a structural breakdown of the model somewhere. Then, you can adjust your SEs and AIC scores by the estimated value of c-hat. However, there are some rules of thumb out there about how large the value of c-hat may be so that you can still take this approach without blushing too much  .... I think the usual upper value is about 3. So, even if you want to take that approach, it might be good to tinker a bit with your model to get a better fit in the first hand.

Best regards  --- Marc

A sexta-feira, 17 de março de 2023 à(s) 13:00:19 UTC, Kery Marc escreveu:
Dear Tiago,

fewer observations don't necessarily mean that you are less likely to get a fitting model in a GoF test like this --- in fact quite the contrary may be true: with less data you have less power to detect patterns that don't look right under your model and are thus less likely to obtain a significant GoF test.

The test output yields at least a little bit of insight into WHERE your model does not fit (at least with respect to time, but not with respect to sites). That is, where the differences between your observed data, and what the model says the data should look like, are greatest.

For the wet season, the total chi-square for the actual data is about 2100, while for a fitting model one would expect a value of about 580 (that's the median of the bootstrap distribution). The value for the full data set is obtained by summing the values of the test statistic over all the years. Thus, under a fitting model one would expect annual values of about 580 / 11 = 53. For the observed data, the chi-square contributions from years 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 look about OK, but for the other years there is strong lack of fit, mostly so in years 4, 7, 8 and 11. Perhaps you can now imagine some process that might have lead to something "special" in these seasons ? And perhaps you can then add a covariate that expresses that effect and in this way improve the fit of your model ?

Finally, you could also adopt what some might say is a dirty little trick, but what is widely done in the analysis of count data: claim that the lack of fit detected is just "overdispersion", or unstructured noise, rather than the result of a structural breakdown of the model somewhere. Then, you can adjust your SEs and AIC scores by the estimated value of c-hat. However, there are some rules of thumb out there about how large the value of c-hat may be so that you can still take this approach without blushing too much  .... I think the usual upper value is about 3. So, even if you want to take that approach, it might be good to tinker a bit with your model to get a better fit in the first hand.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Tiago,

yes, I think the number of occasions or their spacing should be taken account of automatically in an occupancy model.

A common approach to OD is to claim that its causes are benign (i.e., simple noise) and then to account for the resulting added uncertainty by making SEs and CIs larger. Specifically, by multiplying the SEs by the square root of the estimate of c-hat and computing CIs using these 'stretched' versions of SE. As for the AIC, there is an overdispersion-corrected version called QAIC. These methods should be implementable for dynocc models using the AICcmodavg R package.

Best regards  ---- Marc
